catalog_quote: 2 e) Stress Little work has been done on stress in tonal languages of Africa, and my own studies are far from complete. It will be noticed that in Mödö I have found word stress to be penultimate except for two syllable verbs, which have final stress, and three syllable nouns of the tone patterns HHH and LLL, which have initial stress. Since stress is distinct from tone, the phonetic features of stress cannot include a difference of pitch, but are confined to an increase in loudness relative to unstressed syllables, and some slight lengthening of the vowel. Word stress is perturbed considerably by the rhythm or stress pattern of longer utterances, but that is another subject.

At PDF p. 60 = printed p. 49 the section '2 e) Stress' reads exactly as quoted: 'Little work has been done on stress in tonal languages of Africa, and my own studies are far from complete. It will be noticed that in Mödö I have found word stress to be penultimate except for two syllable verbs, which have final stress, and three syllable nouns of the tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mödö is a two-level-tone language with word stress independent of tone: stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (stated separately for VCVCV(CV) verbs, disyllabic and most trisyllabic nouns, adverbs, and pronouns/particles), realised as greater loudness plus slight vowel lengthening. Exceptions: disyllabic (VCV, vowel-prefixed) verbs are stressed on the final syllable; trisyllabic nouns whose tone pattern is all-High or all-Low are stressed on the first syllable; four-syllable nouns carry stress 'on the penultimate and the first syllables'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not labelled as such; for four-syllable nouns the author states 'Stress: on the penultimate and the first syllables' (p.47), i.e. two stresses, without ranking them.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) two-syllable verbs (VCV) — final stress (p.46); (2) three-syllable nouns with tone patterns HHH or LLL — initial stress (p.47); (3) four-syllable nouns — penultimate and first syllables (p.47); (4) when an adverb's final vowel is lengthened for emphasis, stress shifts onto that vowel 'so that it remains penultimate' (sowa -> sowaa, titi -> titii; p.48); author cautions her stress studies are 'far from complete'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is explicitly the word ('the word is.. the domain in which function.. vowel harmony, tone and stress', p.45); statements are for citation forms by word class; author notes word stress 'is perturbed considerably by the rhythm or stress pattern of longer utterances'. Describes the Mödö dialect proper (southern Modo), not Lörï.
new_statements.identity_note: Persson 1981 describes the Mödö dialect proper (southern Jur Modo, the written standard), explicitly one member of the 'Jur dialect cluster' (Mödö, Lori, Sopi, Molo, Gweri, Morokodo, Nyamusa, Wira, Beli); Lörï (also under jurm1239/bex) is mentioned only for consonant differences. Glottocode jurm1239 / ISO bex matches; no dialect-level glottocode needed. Note Glottolog's listing of Scruggs 1980 under jurm1239 is spurious (no Modo content), and Glottolog lacks the key source (J. Persson 1981, OPSL 1: 43-54).

sources.note: The 1991 outline by the same authors as the catalog source (J. Persson 1981) drops the stress section entirely; it neither confirms nor contradicts the penultimate rule. It agrees with 1981 on the two-tone system and V/CV syllable structure that the 1981 stress statement presupposes. The open_url points only to the morsyn-1 (grammar) extract; the Rosetta Project holds three extracts of this dictionary (phon-1, morsyn-1, number-1), all already held by the project, none with a stress statement; the full 148-page dictionary is not online.
